subtype: Shapes in clouds and shadows [Actor]
passage: At outdoor time, five-year-old Payal lay on the school grass and shouted, "A dragon! Look, his tail!" The cloud stretched across the sky, and she roared at it, giggling. After lunch, the nap room was dim. Payal opened her eyes and froze. On the wall, the coat rack's shadow had long arms and a lumpy head. She pulled the sheet over her face and whimpered. Ms Vandana came and knelt. "What do you see?" "A monster." Ms Vandana switched on the small lamp. The monster became hooks and a raincoat. Payal peeked out. "It was a cloud shape," she whispered.

qa.q: What did the coat rack's shadow turn into when the lamp came on?
qa.a: Hooks and a raincoat.

qa.q: How did Payal feel at nap time, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Frightened 😰 She froze, pulled the sheet over her face and whimpered.

qa.q: What did Ms Vandana choose to do, and why did it help?
qa.a: She knelt, asked what Payal saw and switched on the small lamp, so Payal could see for herself that the monster was hooks and a raincoat.

qa.q: What would change if Ms Vandana had only said "There's no monster, go to sleep"?
qa.a: Payal might have stayed scared under the sheet, because she would not have seen the shadow change for herself.

grounding: A preschooler delights in a dragon cloud and later fears a shadow monster, both from seeing shapes.

subtype: Shapes in clouds and shadows [Actor]
passage: I'm Abhinav, and my neighbour Irfan, who's five, sleeps over sometimes. On Saturday evening we lay on the terrace, and Irfan pointed up. "An elephant! With a long nose!" He laughed so much he got hiccups. Later, in my room, the fan made a spinning shadow on the ceiling. Irfan grabbed my arm. "Spider. Big spider." He wouldn't let go. I don't know what he really saw. Maybe the same kind of shapes, just scarier in the dark. I switched the fan off and the shadow stopped. Irfan sighed and fell asleep holding my sleeve.

qa.q: What did Irfan see in the clouds?
qa.a: An elephant with a long nose.

qa.q: What does Irfan grabbing Abhinav's arm suggest?
qa.a: He was scared of the spinning shadow, which looked to him like a big spider.

qa.q: What did Abhinav do that helped Irfan settle?
qa.a: Switched the fan off so the shadow stopped moving, which took away the "spider" without any argument.

qa.q: Why can Abhinav only guess what Irfan saw?
qa.a: Abhinav watches from outside; only Irfan knows what shape he saw in the shadow, and a five-year-old may not be able to explain it.

grounding: A neighbour watches a young child laugh at an elephant cloud and then fear a spider shadow at night.

subtype: Shapes in clouds and shadows [Actor]

"Let's make shadows." She made a dog; Disha made a wobbly bird. Then Disha pointed at the curtain. "That's just a curtain witch. She's friends with my bird." She giggled and switched the torch off.

qa.a: Much less scared 🙂 She called it "just a curtain witch" who is friends with her bird, and giggled.

subtype: Lucky shirt, lucky pen [Actor]
passage: Nazia's school kho-kho team won the district match in Barpeta on the day she wore her faded green T-shirt under the jersey. Since then, the green shirt had come to every match. Four more wins. Nazia refused to let Ammi wash it in match weeks. "It knows the game," she told Bidisha on the bus. Then Ammi washed it by mistake, and they lost to the team from the next block. Nazia sat on the bench, furious at the soap. Bidisha nudged her. "Their captain was twice as fast as last year, na? And Rumi was sick." Nazia stared at the damp shirt on the line. "Still. It's the shirt." But she didn't sound quite as sure.

subtype: Lucky shirt, lucky pen [Actor]
passage: In Kumasi, sixteen-year-old Kwame got the top mark in his class on a maths test, and he had written it with a chewed blue pen he'd found on the bus. After that, the blue pen came to every test. Physics: a good mark. History: good. Kwame kept it in a separate pocket, wrapped in a tissue. The night before chemistry, the pen ran dry. He shook it, breathed on it, scribbled on his palm. Nothing. His younger sister Rania watched from the doorway. "You studied, right?" "Yes, but the pen..." "The pen didn't study." She tossed him a black one. Kwame turned it over in his fingers, uneasy. Next day his hand shook a little on the first question. Then he remembered the formulas, and it steadied.

qa.q: Where had Kwame found the blue pen?
qa.a: On the bus.

qa.q: Why did Kwame feel uneasy holding the black pen?
qa.a: He had linked his good marks to the blue pen, so writing without it felt like losing his luck, even though he had studied.

qa.q: What turning point showed Kwame what really carried him in the chemistry test?
qa.a: When he remembered the formulas and his hand steadied: the studying, not the pen, was doing the work.

qa.q: How does Rania see Kwame's panic over the pen?
qa.a: Rania seems to find it a little silly and reminds him that "the pen didn't study"; the credit belongs to Kwame's own work.

grounding: A teenage boy credits a lucky pen for his marks and panics when it runs dry, reading cause into coincidence.

passage: At the badminton club, everyone knew about Vandana's socks: yellow, with a hole at the left toe. She had worn them for her first tournament win in March, and now she refused to play a serious match without them. Today she arrived late and red-faced. "Coach, I couldn't find them. I'm going to lose." Coach Madhuri didn't laugh. She opened the scorebook. "Let's look. Five matches in those socks since March. Three wins, two losses. And two wins in other socks." Vandana frowned at the page. "But the first win..." "Was the week you practised your smash every evening," said Madhuri. Vandana looked down at her plain white socks. She still felt jittery walking on court. But she remembered the smash.

qa.a: Five matches since March: three wins, two losses.

qa.q: What was Vandana feeling when she arrived without the socks?
qa.a: Panicky and sure she would lose 😰 She was red-faced and felt as if her luck was missing.

qa.a: It checked the socks against real results, showing wins and losses in them and wins without them, and pointed Vandana back to her practice.

qa.q: What would change if Coach Madhuri had laughed at the socks?

grounding: A teenage player believes her socks bring wins after one tournament, and her coach checks the belief against the scorebook.

subtype: Seeing hidden plans in coincidences [Actor]
passage: Sahil had it all on a sticky note by his hostel bed. The Wi-Fi dropped on the three nights before exams. The canteen ran out of paneer on the days fest meetings were called. The warden's scooter was parked at the admin block every time. "It's a plan," he told Dolma, his wingmate, eyes bright. "They want us distracted. Nobody else has noticed." He liked that part: the feeling of seeing what others missed. Dolma listened, then took out her own phone. "Let's test it. I'll note every Wi-Fi drop this month, exam or not." Three weeks later she showed him the list: eleven drops, only three near exams. Paneer ran out on random days. The warden's scooter was at admin almost daily. Sahil read it twice, a little deflated. "Huh. It looked so neat."

qa.q: How many Wi-Fi drops did Dolma note, and how many were near exams?
qa.a: Eleven drops, only three near exams.

qa.a: The feeling of seeing what others missed; he felt special for having noticed a secret plan.

qa.a: Dolma may have been doubtful but kind, choosing to test it together rather than mock it.

grounding: A hostel student strings unrelated events into a secret plan and feels special, until a wingmate tests it against a month of records.

subtype: Seeing hidden plans in coincidences [Actor]
passage:
Samir bhai,
You'll laugh, but I have to tell someone. For two weeks I've been seeing 17 everywhere. The bus I take is 17. My exam seat was 17. Our old hostel room was 17. I started thinking it meant something, like the universe was lining things up for me. Honestly, it felt amazing, like being let in on a secret.
Then I remembered your line: "What would it look like if it were just chance?" So yesterday I wrote down every number I noticed from morning to night. Forty-three numbers. Three were 17. I'd only remembered the 17s because I was hunting for them.
So, no cosmic message. Just my brain collecting hits and ignoring misses. Slightly sad, weirdly relieving. Come home soon. The bus is still 17.
Kunal

passage: Tenzin, it's Nirmala's confession time. Last semester I cracked a code, or thought I did. Professor Rao tells a lot of bad jokes in thermodynamics, right? I felt like a genius, like I'd seen what the whole class was missing. I started writing his jokes in the margin with stars. I even told two friends to study "by the jokes". Then before the final you asked me, "How many jokes didn't turn into questions?" I went back through my notes. Thirty-one jokes. Two matched. Two! The rest were about cricket and his cat. I felt a bit silly, but mostly relieved I hadn't skipped chapters for it. I studied everything after that.

qa.a: Thirty-one jokes, and two matched.

subtype: Testing the pattern before believing it [Response]
passage: "You're up again?" Ritu found her sister Kalyani on the balcony at 3:40 am. "It was 3:33 when I woke up. Third time this month. And every time, something goes wrong the next day." "Like what?" "The bus broke down. Amma's knee hurt. The laptop crashed." Ritu sat down. "Didi, things go wrong most days." Kalyani laughed weakly. "I know. That's what I keep telling myself. So here's my plan. For two weeks I'll write down every time I wake up, whatever the time, and whether the next day is bad." "And if it's the same with 2:10 or 4:50?" "Then it's just me noticing the scary number." Kalyani pulled her shawl tighter. "And if it keeps frightening me like this, I'll book the counsellor at work. I don't want to lie awake counting." "I'll remind you," said Ritu.

qa.q: What time was it when Kalyani woke up?
qa.a: 3:33, for the third time that month.

qa.q: How was Kalyani feeling on the balcony, and what shows it?
qa.a: Uneasy and a bit frightened. She was awake at 3:40 am, laughed weakly and pulled her shawl tighter.

qa.q: What plan did Kalyani make, and why is it a sound one?
qa.a: To log every waking time and whether the next day went badly for two weeks, so 3:33 can be compared with chance, and to book the work counsellor if the fear keeps up.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel finding Kalyani on the balcony?
qa.a: Ritu seems concerned but steady, offering an ordinary explanation and promising to help by reminding Kalyani about the counsellor.

subtype: Testing the pattern before believing it [Response]
passage: I'm Preeti, and last spring I became convinced my manager, Vijay, was watching my screen. Every time I opened a job site on my lunch break, an email from him seemed to land within minutes. It happened on Monday. Then Wednesday. My stomach dropped each time. I started closing tabs and jumping at notification sounds. One evening I made myself ask: what would this look like if it were just chance? He sends dozens of emails a day. So for two weeks I noted every time I opened the site and every email from him, matched or not. Twenty-six emails. Four near my breaks. The rest came at any time at all. That helped. But I was still tense, still scanning for signs, and it was wearing me out. So I booked a session with a counsellor. Talking it through helped more than any spreadsheet.

subtype: Testing the pattern before believing it [Response]
passage: Supervisor's note, analytics team. Jagdish. Afreen, 24, came to me on Tuesday, excited. In last quarter's data, customer complaints seemed to jump every time our radio advert played. First, she asked, "What would this look like if it were just luck?" and shuffled the advert dates randomly a hundred times; similar jumps turned up in about a third of the shuffles. Second, she waited for this month's data as a fresh test. The link vanished. She was disappointed, and said so, but she binned the chart. She also told me that late nights staring at charts had left her jittery, seeing links in everything, so she has booked a session with the company counsellor. I told her both were good decisions.

qa.a: They might have changed or blamed the radio advert based on a chance pattern, wasting time and money.

subtype: Glee when the sibling is scolded [Actor]
passage: "Uday, it's dark! I said home by six!" Mumma's voice filled the doorway. "Sorry, Mumma, the match went on..." Behind the sofa, six-year-old Pallavi giggled. "Pallavi, is this funny?" The giggle stopped. "No." "Then why are you smiling?" Pallavi picked at a sofa thread. "He always gets to go out late. I never do." Mumma sat down. "So you were glad he's in trouble?" Pallavi nodded, shook her head, nodded again. "A little. Now I feel bad." Uday sniffed. "Thanks a lot." "Sorry, bhaiya." Mumma pulled them both close. "Tomorrow, Pallavi comes to the match too. Till six."

passage: Vikas, it's Sunaina's turn to confess something ugly. You know the auditions for the annual play? Mihir had been telling everyone for weeks that the lead was "basically his". subtype: Rival's failure feels good and bad [Actor]
passage: I'm Ojas, Harish's classmate. On Friday the district band results went up on the music-room door. Harish's grin went. He stared at the floor for a while. On the bus he was quiet, and I saw him type something to Neel. I don't know what it said, or whether he felt guilty or just awkward. But he didn't join the jokes at the back of the bus.

qa.a: On the music-room door.

passage: The mid-semester marks went up on the notice board of their Bengaluru college, and a small crowd formed. Megha, top of the class for three semesters, had scraped a 61 in Signals. Francis nudged Samir, trying not to grin. "Miss Perfect finally slipped." He said it low, but his eyes were shining. Samir looked at the board, then at Francis. He didn't laugh. Later, walking to the canteen, he asked, "Why does her 61 make you so happy?" Francis shrugged. "She makes it look easy. I study till two and still get 70." "So it's more about you than her?" Francis kicked a stone. "Maybe. Yeah." They bought tea. Francis didn't mention Megha again.

qa.q: What mark did Megha get in Signals?
What was Francis feeling under the grin?
qa.a: Envy and frustration: he studies till two and still gets 70, so Megha's slip felt satisfying because she makes it look easy.

qa.a: He stayed quiet at the board and later gently asked why the 61 made Francis so happy, which helped Francis see it was about his own struggle.

qa.a: She would likely feel hurt and isolated, already dealing with a low mark and now being enjoyed by classmates.

grounding: A student sees Francis enjoy a top student's low mark and, instead of joining in, gently asks what the envy is about.

subtype: Friend notices glee at another's downfall [Observer]
passage: "Did you see? Dev's project got rejected by the department. Mister Gold Medal." Kamal was grinning over his phone in the library corridor. Arohi kept her voice low. "You look really pleased." "I'm not pleased. It's just funny. He always acts like he's above everyone." "Did he act like that with you?" "Not exactly. He just... gets everything." "Mm." Arohi waited. "If you could have one of his things, what would it be?" Kamal was quiet. "The professor asking my opinion. The way he asks Dev." "That's a real thing to want." "Yeah." Kamal put the phone away. "Don't tell anyone I was gloating." "You weren't, really. You were jealous. Different." "Wow, thanks." But he was almost smiling.

qa.q: Where were Arohi and Kamal talking?
qa.a: In the library corridor.

qa.q: What did Kamal really want, underneath the gloating?

I didn't laugh. I didn't lecture him either. I just stayed quiet and went down the stairs. Kunal caught up with me. "What, too mean?" "Kind of," I said. "Is it about Farzana, or about the interviews?" He went quiet. Then he admitted he'd been turned down by two colleges and she had got into both. Looking back, I'm glad I didn't join in. It was easier than I thought, just not laughing.

But I saw two colleagues by the tea urn, smiling at each other when I walked in and stopping when I came near. I ate lunch alone at my desk for a month. I felt the size of a pin.
